rv.q: A prodigious theatrical event that aims for greatness and achieves it, this revival of the Stephen Sondheim-Hugh Wheeler masterpiece is not to be missed.

At once funny, scary and disarmingly moving, this must-see production is content to peel back any cobwebs or artifice and let Stephen Sondheim and Hugh Wheeler’s Gothic revenge tragedy of a musical howl anew with the agony of human injustice and the ameliorating constancy of love.
Now comes a new special on the menu: the ravishingly sung, deeply emotional and strangely hilarious 'Sweeney'
Regardless, all it takes is a swell of the orchestra and the hellfire wails of the chorus to joltingly remind us we’re at one of the greatest musicals ever written.
The choices the production makes will divide “Sweeney Todd” purists, who have grown accustomed to hollowed-out killing machines in the title role.
It’s a close-shave approach to the role: clean and precise, it doesn’t pierce the surface.
Sondheim's Grand Guignol masterwork sounds as grand here as it deserves to.

Kail, riding high after directing Hamilton, aims to ratchet Sweeney all the way back up, deploying a cast of 25, a two-level set by Mimi Lien with a towering crane — going big and crucially, expressionistic.

Beauty, horror, innocence, humor: By some mysterious alchemy, “Sweeney Todd” excels at illuminating them all, exploring the best and worst of humanity in one of musical theater’s most thrilling, and chilling, works.
Thomas Kail is the latest director to take a stab at Sondheim’s epic — pumping thrilling life into a macabre Broadway revival.
When he swings his razor high, the hair on the back of your neck doesn't budge.
Sonically thrilling, yes, but a frolicking Lovett and her sad Sweeney couldn’t, in the end, chill my blood.
The result is something both sumptuous and terrifying, truly a Sweeney Todd for the ages.
When onstage together, Ashford and Groban are a force to be reckoned with as they bring the painfully one-sided relationship between their characters to life.
This spine-tingling revival delivers that, and so much more.
In that closing moment—like much of the show, thrilling and arch all at once—an exquisite production outdid itself.
Unlike Lovett's repugnant meat pies, there's nothing half-baked about this "Sweeney Todd," which in its stunning final moments, reminds you just how exhilarating live theater can be.

The answers, as it turns out, are yes and yes. Groban proved his stage acting chops in a vastly different role a few years ago, in the Broadway premiere of the musical “Natasha, Pierre & the Great Comet of 1812,” his Sweeney is more of a revelation, showing an agility and depth that should put any accusations of stunt casting to rest.
She’s hilarious—and extremely handsy with Sweeney—but, regrettably, not at all villainous.

A fully staged “Sweeney Todd” opened Sunday at Broadway’s Lunt-Fontanne Theatre, and beyond the aforementioned concert version, it is the best sung version of the Stephen Sondheim and Hugh Wheeler musical I’ve ever heard.
Absent that, or even a faint whiff of borderline madness from what he’s been dealt, the production comes off as a bit too tame.
Sweeney Todd, then, can still shock, even if this production seldom goes for the jugular.
Josh Groban and Annaleigh Ashford star in a revival that brings new energy to Stephen Sondheim's murderous musical masterpiece.

The marvel of Sondheim’s creation, the magnificence of the score and Tunick’s orchestrations, the superb performances, and the cumulative power of Kail’s production all combine to make this Sweeney Todd what promises to be the most memorable production of the 2023 theater season . . . and beyond.

cn.t: Critics praise this sumptuous, full-scale revival for Groban and Ashford's powerful performances and the lush 26-piece orchestra, though some find the production lacks the darkest edge Sondheim's masterpiece demands.
